newsitem.title: LUXEMBOURG: FOCUS - EU, Nordics to seek alcohol deal next week.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - EU, Nordics to seek alcohol deal next week.

text.p: The European Commission said on Monday there had been progress in sensitive talks on phasing out rules that allow the three Nordic EU members to limit the alcohol people may bring back home from elsewhere in the bloc.
The European Union executive and Denmark, Sweden and Finland will seek to reach a deal in principle at a new meeting scheduled for Wednesday next week.

"It is clear that we meet because we still believe there is a possibility to find agreement," Swedish Finance Minister Erik Asbrink told reporters after Monday's talks. "But it is far from certain," he added.

EU Internal Market Commissioner Mario Monti met with Asbrink, Finnish Finance Minister Sauli Niinisto and Danish Economy Minister Marianne Jelved on the sidelines of a meeting of EU finance ministers in Luxembourg.
"I saw some signs of movement in their position," Monti told reporters.
Finland's Niinisto also said there had been movement, adding he hoped there would be a solution already next week. "I hope that we can find a compromise," he told Reuters.
However, Asbrink said there was still disagreement on the controversial issue. "We've had an exchange of views and we are not in agreement," he said.
Finnish Prime Minister Paavo Lipponen said this month that Sweden, Finland and Denmark want to keep their restrictions on personal alcohol imports unchanged until at least 1999.

However, such a position would be unlikely to go down well with Monti, who is pushing for a fixed date when the Nordics' special import restrictions should end altogether. "On the date I stressed once again the need to have one," Monti said.

Denmark, Sweden and Finland all have exemptions from EU rules so that they can restrict imports of cheaper alcohol, but these will expire by the end of 1996 unless there is a new agreement -- at least according to the Commission.

The Commission wants the restrictions to end because it says they go against the internal market -- where goods are supposed to flow freely -- while the Nordics want to keep them because of health- and tax-reasons.

The issue is politically sensitive for the Nordic states which have a traditional policy of high taxes on alcohol as part of efforts to reduce excessive drinking. It is also a question of fiscal importance as the taxes bring in much needed revenue.
Asbrink said Sweden had "strong reasons" to continue to pursue a restrictive alcohol policy. "We are trying to convince the Commission that this is an important question," he said.

A compromise leading to a phasing out of the restrictions would gradually allow Swedes, Finns and Danes to bring in more alcohol while at the same giving the three Nordics time to prepare for the new rules, according to the Commission.
But as Nordic excise duties on alcohol are much higher than elsewhere in the EU, some fear individual alcohol imports would jump if the Nordics lost their right to restrict imports.
Under current rules, a Swede is allowed to take home up to one litre of spirits, five litres of wine and 15 litres of beer, much less than most other EU citizens.
